rounds.text: RBZ Jewellers Ltd trades at a compelling P/E ratio of 13.3x [E1], representing a steep discount to the broader sector benchmark of 26.79x [E6]. This valuation disconnect stands in stark contrast to the company's powerful growth metrics, including a 5-year compounded sales growth of 43% [E14] and a TTM profit growth of 54% [E19]. Furthermore, a discounted cash flow model indicates an intrinsic value of Rs 579 per share against the market price of Rs 188 [E39], leaving an enormous margin of safety of 67.5% [E40]. Operational efficiency is equally robust, demonstrated by a superior return on equity of 18.28% against a sector benchmark of 8.42% [E9] and a ROCE of 18.74% [E10]. The rules-based screen also awards the stock a high score of 89 out of 100 on the back of surging year-on-year sales and profit figures [E56, E57, E59]. Conceded: operating cash flow turned negative at Rs -7 Cr for Mar 2026 along with an FCF of Rs -40 Cr [E28, E29, E30]. Nevertheless, the company is actively expanding its retail footprint with new store launches scheduled across Gujarat [E74], and management anticipates strong consumer demand moving forward [E71].

The primary risk in RBZ Jewellers lies in its severe cash flow generation disconnect, evidenced by a cash conversion ratio of -0.13x and negative operating cash flow of Rs -7 Cr for March 2026 [E28, E29]. Free cash flow sits at an alarming Rs -40 Cr [E30], with operating cash flow representing a mere 13% of operating profit [E31], raising questions about the quality of reported earnings. This cash burn coincides with a heavy capital expenditure and debt build-up phase, as borrowings jumped to Rs 170 Cr in March 2026 from Rs 91 Cr a year earlier [E33], and Capital Work in Progress surged by 733.3% to Rs 25 Cr [E34]. Furthermore, institutional confidence has evaporated, evidenced by foreign institutions slashing their holdings from 4.33% to 0.03% and domestic institutions dropping from 3.03% to 0.01% since December 2023 [E36, E37]. Operating margins have also turned volatile, contracting by 2 percentage points year-on-year to 15% in June 2026 [E25] and reading inconsistent on both yearly and quarterly horizons [E26, E27]. Conceded: the company boasts robust historical sales and profit growth alongside strong return metrics like an 18.28% ROE and an 18.74% ROCE that exceed sector benchmarks [E9, E10, E14, E17].

Conceded: cash conversion is negative at -0.13x with operating cash flow at Rs -7 Cr and free cash flow at Rs -40 Cr [E28, E29, E30]. However, this cash burn and the surge in CWIP by 733.3% to Rs 25 Cr directly reflect an active growth and capex build-up phase—supported by a sanctioned debt of Rs 300 crores—designed to fund four new retail stores including Surat, Rajkot, Maninagar, and Gandhinagar this financial year [E34, E74, E83]. Conceded: borrowings rose to Rs 170 Cr [E33] and institutional holdings declined [E36, E37], but management explicitly anticipates that the debt-to-equity ratio will remain a healthy below 1:1 at around 0.8 to 1 by the end of the financial year [E69]. While the bear points to a two percentage point quarterly margin contraction to 15% in June 2026 [E25], the company simultaneously delivered a 39% year-on-year EBITDA growth to INR 18 crores with a healthy 14.9% margin [E77] and robust revenue growth of approximately 60% driven by strong customer demand [E72]. Furthermore, the strategic B2B to B2C shift targeting a 50-50 mix in a year or two [E68] and swift capex break-even expected in a year or less for the new stores [E70] completely offset short-term margin fluctuations.

While the bull frames negative cash flow as a byproduct of growth [E34], the reality is a negative cash conversion of -0.13x [E28] and a free cash flow deficit of Rs -40 Cr [E30], where operating cash flow represents only 13% of operating profit [E31]. Conceded: management targets a debt-to-equity ratio below 1:1 for the current year [E69], but borrowings have already nearly doubled to Rs 170 Cr [E33], and the stated plan to eventually leverage up to 2:1 [E84] creates a precarious financial profile regardless of current sanctioned limits [E83]. The bull dismisses the institutional exodus, yet the near-total liquidation of holdings by foreign institutions from 4.33% to 0.03% [E36] and domestic institutions from 3.03% to 0.01% [E37] signals a profound lack of professional confidence [E38, E62]. Robust revenue growth [E72] is undermined by a two-percentage-point drop in quarterly operating margins [E25], an inconsistent yearly margin trend [E26], and decelerating earnings growth [E61]. Finally, reliance on optimistic break-even targets [E70, E88] ignores the company's own warning that results may differ [E85] and the stock's history of extreme 62.0% volatility [E48] and a -57.4% peak-to-trough drawdown [E47].

The bear’s focus on negative cash flow [E28, E30] overlooks that these deficits are driven by a massive 733.3% surge in capital work-in-progress [E34] and the heavy inventory requirements of up to Rs 150 Cr per new large-format store [E75] as the company aggressively pivots toward a 75% retail revenue mix [E68]. Conceded: borrowings have increased [E33] and institutional holdings have sharply declined [E36, E37], yet the current debt-to-equity ratio remains moderate at 0.57x [E32], and management expects to maintain this below 1:1 through the financial year [E69, E87]. While the bear highlights a quarterly margin dip [E25], the trailing twelve-month (TTM) operating margin has actually expanded by 2 percentage points over three years [E24], supporting a robust TTM profit growth of 54% [E19]. This fundamental strength is reflected in a relative-strength rating of 100 against the Nifty 500 [E45] and a rules-based buy score of 89/100 [E56]. Furthermore, the bear’s concerns regarding volatility [E48] are mitigated by a significant 67.5% margin of safety [E40], with the stock trading at a P/E of 13.67x—nearly half the sector benchmark of 26.79x [E6]. With four new stores launching this year [E74] and expected to reach capex break-even in a year or less [E70, E88], the current 60% YoY revenue growth [E57, E72] suggests the market is significantly under-appreciating the company's expansion phase.

The bull dismisses the negative cash flow as merely a consequence of growth [E28, E30, E34], but ignores the sheer scale of the cash burn, which hit negative Rs 40 Cr in Free Cash Flow [E30] alongside a cash conversion ratio of -0.13x [E28]. Conceded: the company is expanding its retail footprint [E68, E74], but borrowings have nearly doubled from Rs 91 Cr to Rs 170 Cr in just one year [E33], and management explicitly plans to leverage up the debt-to-equity ratio as high as 1.5 or 2:1 using Gold Metal Loans [E84]. While the bull points to a rising 3-year operating margin trend [E24], it glosses over the immediate deterioration showing quarterly operating margins contracting by 2 percentage points year-on-year [E25] within an inconsistent margin pattern [E26, E27]. Furthermore, the bull's reliance on relative strength and high scores [E45, E56] completely fails to address the severe institutional exodus, evidenced by foreign and domestic institutional holdings plunging by 4.30 and 3.02 percentage points respectively [E36, E37] to near-zero levels. Finally, citing a large margin of safety from a DCF model [E40] does not protect investors from an annualized volatility of 62.0% [E48] and a historical maximum drawdown of -57.4% [E47].
